**Observation Log:**

- [TEMPORAL] Session Date: 2023/06/18 (Sun) 02:16
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The case discussed is Prime Constructions Pty Ltd v Westbridge Investments Pty Ltd, heard in the Supreme Court of New South Wales in 2004.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The case involved a dispute over a settlement agreement for goods sold and delivered.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The plaintiff filed a statement of liquidated claim for $11,754.60 in the Local Court, which was disputed by the defendant.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Both parties were represented by solicitors.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] On 21 January 2004, the plaintiff's solicitor made an offer to settle for the amount claimed, with each party to pay its own costs.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The defendant's solicitor accepted the offer on 23 January 2004, and a deed of release was agreed upon.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The defendant later proposed an additional term regarding a letter from the plaintiff about the quality of the works done, leading to further correspondence.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The central issue was whether there was a final settlement of the proceedings.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The court found there was a final settlement, as the terms of the deed and settlement had been agreed upon.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The court considered a document executed on 9 February 2004, which was in the form of a deed.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The court found the deed was not properly executed according to the Corporations Act and the Conveyancing Act.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The court held that the deed took effect from the date of delivery on 12 February 2004, due to estoppel or ratification.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The court declared the defendant was bound by the terms of the deed of release and ordered the defendant to pay the plaintiff $11,721.60.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The defendant was also ordered to pay the plaintiff's costs of the proceedings.
- [USER] Asked about the issues with the deed in the case.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The deed was expressed to be a deed but was not properly executed as only one director of the plaintiff company signed it.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Under the Corporations Act 2001 and the Conveyancing Act 1919, a company must have two directors or a director and a company secretary sign a deed.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The plaintiff argued the deed was binding because it had been delivered to the defendant's solicitor and the plaintiff was willing to perform its part of the agreement
